script.analysis: All 18,554 stored characters read in two contiguous ranges with canonical hash match. Hook: 3% raise eaten by inflation, stagnation framed as decisions not made; early subscribe/like CTA. Fourteen traps delivered sequentially with brief explanations: (1) employer not your friend + 12-year loyalty anecdote, (2) tenure plateau and job-switch premium, (3) market-value research tools, (4) not asking, (5) risk aversion, (6) first offers, (7) busy vs high-impact, (8) firm-specific skills, (9) waiting for permission, (10) experience vs repetition, (11) networking, (12) staying in lane, (13) benefits negotiation, (14) imagined ceilings; close "in 5 years". List structure with numbered signposting and almost no data, sources or worked negotiation examples; one anecdote. Advice is mostly mainstream career guidance but presented with absolute claims ("guarantee", "most ceilings are imaginary") and no acknowledgment of labor-market, credential, location or discrimination constraints. ASR artifacts ("9-to-F5", "ER8s") preserved; not audio-verified.

beat_map.beat: 3%-raise hook, CTA, traps 1-6: employer incentives and loyalty anecdote, tenure plateau and switching math, market value tools, asking, risk, first offer
Traps 7-14: busy work, transferable skills, permission, experience, network, lane, benefits, imagined ceilings; 5-year guarantee close

claim_audit: 0:9500 $40,000 to $50,000 over 12 years = ~1.88%/year (script "basically 2%"), correct; whether that lags inflation depends on the period (2010s US CPI averaged ~1.8-2%, so roughly flat, not clearly negative). "30% bump by switching" a few years ago and "20% premium" today are unsourced; Atlanta Fed Wage Growth Tracker data show job switchers' median annual wage growth only a few percentage points above stayers even at the 2022 peak, so 20-30% per move is not typical. Four 20% jumps in 10 years = 2.07x versus 3%/year 10 years = 1.34x - arithmetic correct but premised on the unsupported 20% figure.

0:9500 "Company's goal is to pay you as little as possible" is a simplification (retention, morale and market rates also matter). "$50,000 left on the table" is an unquantified possibility. Glassdoor, Payscale and LinkedIn salary data are real tools but self-reported and noisy - presented as "real numbers from real people" without caveats. Offers often have budget room, but "everything is negotiable" overstates for structured pay scales (government, unions).

9500:18554 Traps 7-14 are qualitative; claims like "Python developer valuable everywhere" and "most ceilings are imaginary" are unsupported generalizations; the closing "I guarantee" outcome promise is not supportable. No tax, statistical or product claims requiring primary-source checks.
